What changed when we stopped roasting to a curve

Three years of logs, one uncomfortable conclusion, and the batch that finally made the argument for us.

The short version

We had been chasing a reference profile for so long that nobody could say what it was for. It described a bean we no longer bought, on a machine we had replaced, for a grind we had stopped recommending. Every batch was measured against it and every deviation was treated as a defect.

412batches logged
-19%development time
2.1×repeat orders

The change was not a new curve. It was dropping the idea that one curve should survive a change of bean, and writing down what we actually tasted instead of what we expected to.

What the logs said

Once we sorted by cup score rather than by adherence, the pattern was immediate and slightly embarrassing. The batches people reordered were the ones that had drifted.

“The profile was never the product. It was a record of one good morning that we kept re-enacting.”

How we roast now

Each origin gets its own target and its own stopping rule, written before the first batch and revised only against the cupping table. Nothing is compared to last year. The log is a diary, not a contract.

The part that took longest was cultural rather than technical: agreeing that a batch which tastes better but reads worse is a better batch. That sentence is easy to write and hard to sign off on at 6am with a roaster already at charge temperature.

What we would do differently

Start with the cupping table. We spent two of the three years collecting data against a question nobody had asked, and the answer only appeared once we changed the question.

And keep the logs public. Half the value turned out to be wholesale customers reading them and telling us which batches they wanted again, which is not information a curve can carry.
